newsitem.title: JAPAN: Nippon Credit to issue 51 bln yen preferred stock.
newsitem.headline: Nippon Credit to issue 51 bln yen preferred stock.

text.p: Nippon Credit Bank Ltd said on Tuesday that it would issue 51 billion yen worth of preferred stock.
The new issue will be Nippon Credit's second preferred share issue and take the form of a third-party allocation, the bank said in a statement.
It said it would issue 102 million shares at 500 yen each.
The pay-in date is set for September 30.
The Bank for International Settlements requires internationally active banks to have a capital-adequacy ratio of 8.0 percent or above.

Nippon Credit Bank, the smallest of Japan's three long-term credit banks, lost 131.1 billion yen in the fiscal year that ended in March 31, 1996, after writing off 421.3 billion yen to cover bad loans.
As a result, the bank's group capital-adequacy ratio declined sharply to 8.38 percent as of the end of March, down from 9.11 percent a year earlier.
The dividend for the preferred shares would be 13.75 yen per year, of which 6.875 yen would be paid as an interim dividend, the bank said.
Officials at the bank were not immediately available for further comment.
The Japanese economic daily Nihon Keizai Shimbun said the bank was planning the issue to boost its capital adequacy ratio.
Japanese banks are considering measures to comply with capital adequacy rules set up under the Bank for International Settlements and to restructure their management bases.
In its efforts to improve its capital adequacy ratio, Nippon Credit issued 50 billion yen in preferred securities through its overseas unit Nippon Credit Bank (Curacao) Capital NV in late August.

But Japanese media said Japan's Finance Ministry, which checks securities issued by banks' units suspected to be paper companies, was reluctant to allow Nippon Credit to include the securities in the prime components of the rule.
The issue of additional preferred stocks announced on Tuesday is expected to make it possible for Nippon Credit to successfully boost its capital adequacy ratio, the Nihon Keizai said.
